Task 1 — Introduction, History, Pipelines and Tokenizer¶

First sentiment pipeline¶

In [6]:
sentiment_pipe = pipeline(
    "sentiment-analysis",
    model="distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english",
    device=-1
)
sentences = [
    "I really enjoyed this movie.",
    "The service was terrible.",
    "The food was not bad at all.",
    "The story was okay, but the ending was disappointing.",
    "I expected to hate it, but I loved it."
]
for sentence in sentences:
    result = sentiment_pipe(sentence)[0]
    print(f"Text: {sentence}\nLabel: {result['label']} | Score: {result['score']:.4f}\n")

Introduction and history¶

In [7]:
history = pd.DataFrame([
    [2014, "Sequence-to-sequence with attention (Bahdanau)", "Attention helped a decoder focus on relevant encoder states."],
    [2015, "Luong attention", "Introduced practical attention scoring methods for neural translation."],

Year Model or paper Why it mattered

Impact and disadvantages¶

Impact: translation, search, chat assistants, code completion, image models, and protein-structure prediction.
Disadvantages: attention can be expensive for long sequences, context windows are limited, models can require large compute and datasets, generated text can hallucinate, and internal decisions can be difficult to interpret.

Interpretation: Transformers are useful for many language tasks. However, their results and running time should always be checked.

Tokenizer in action¶

Tokenizers turn text into model-readable token pieces and integer IDs. Sub-word tokenization can represent rare words by splitting them into smaller familiar pieces.

In [8]:
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english")
text = "Transformers are surprisingly easy to understand."
enc = tok(text)
print("Tokens:", tok.tokenize(text))
print("Input IDs:", enc["input_ids"])
print("Attention mask:", enc["attention_mask"])
print("Special tokens:", tok.convert_ids_to_tokens(enc["input_ids"]))
print("Long/rare word pieces:", tok.tokenize("unbelievably"))
print("[CLS] starts a sequence and [SEP] separates/ends a sequence for this tokenizer.")

Attention mask: [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]
Special tokens: ['[CLS]', 'transformers', 'are', 'surprisingly', 'easy', 'to', 'understand', '.', '[SEP]']

Interpretation: A tokenizer changes text into tokens and numbers. Sub-word tokens help the model handle unfamiliar words.

Batching and padding¶

Padding makes sentences in a batch the same length. The attention mask uses 1 for real tokens and 0 for padding tokens

In [9]:
batch_texts = ["Transformers are useful.", "Transformers can model relationships between words in a sentence."]
batch = tok(batch_texts, padding=True, return_tensors="pt")
print("Tokens:")
for row in batch["input_ids"]:
    print(tok.convert_ids_to_tokens(row.tolist()))
print("\nInput IDs:\n", batch["input_ids"])
print("\nAttention mask:\n", batch["attention_mask"])

Task 2 — Self-Attention and Scaled Dot-Product Attention¶

Self-attention idea¶

Each token is projected into a Query (what it looks for), Key (what it offers) and Value (information to pass along). Query–Key scores become weights, and each token receives a weighted combination of Value vectors. All tokens can be processed in parallel.

Interpretation: Self-attention helps each word use information from other words. Query, Key, and Value are used to calculate attention.

Scaled dot-product attention from scratch¶

The score matrix compares each query with every key. Dividing by the square root of the key size keeps scores from becoming excessively large before softmax.

In [11]:
def softmax(x, axis=-1):
    x = x - np.max(x, axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    e = np.exp(x)
    return e / np.sum(e, axis=axis, keepdims=True)

np.random.seed(42)
X = np.random.randn(4, 8)
Wq, Wk, Wv = [np.random.randn(8, 8) for _ in range(3)]
Q, K, V = X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv
scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(8)
weights = softmax(scores)
out = weights @ V
print("X:", X.shape, "Q:", Q.shape, "K:", K.shape, "V:", V.shape)
print("Scores:", scores.shape, "Weights:", weights.shape, "Output:", out.shape)
print("Row sums:", weights.sum(axis=1))
plt.figure(figsize=(5, 4))
sns.heatmap(weights, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="Blues")
plt.title("Task 2.2 — NumPy Attention Weights")
plt.xlabel("Key token"); plt.ylabel("Query token"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

X: (4, 8) Q: (4, 8) K: (4, 8) V: (4, 8)
Scores: (4, 4) Weights: (4, 4) Output: (4, 8)
Row sums: [1. 1. 1. 1.]

Interpretation: Softmax changes attention scores into probabilities. Each row of the attention matrix should add up to about 1.

Why divide by square root of d_k?¶

This experiment compares softmax probabilities with and without scaling for key sizes 4 and 256. Entropy is included as a measure of how spread out each row's attention is.

In [12]:
np.random.seed(42)
rows = []
for dk in [4, 256]:
    q = np.random.randn(100, dk)
    k = np.random.randn(100, dk)
    raw = q @ k.T
    for scaled in [False, True]:
        s = raw / np.sqrt(dk) if scaled else raw
        p = softmax(s, axis=-1)
        ent = -(p * np.log(p + 1e-12)).sum(axis=-1).mean()
        rows.append([dk, "With scaling" if scaled else "Without scaling",
                     p.max(axis=-1).mean(), ent])
display(pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["d_k", "Method", "Mean row maximum", "Mean entropy"]))
d_k Method Mean row maximum Mean entropy
0 4 Without scaling 0.212706 3.292038
1 4 With scaling 0.070224 4.179688
2 256 Without scaling 0.875729 0.294367
3 256 With scaling 0.081190 4.127719

Interpretation: Large dot products can make attention focus too strongly on a few tokens. Scaling helps keep the attention scores more balanced.

Self-attention vs Luong attention¶

Luong dot attention uses one decoder state to score several encoder states. It is different from self-attention, where each token in a sequence attends to tokens in that same sequence.

In [13]:
np.random.seed(42)
encoder_states = np.random.randn(5, 8)
decoder_state = np.random.randn(8)
luong_scores = encoder_states @ decoder_state
luong_weights = softmax(luong_scores)
context = luong_weights @ encoder_states
print("Luong weights:", np.round(luong_weights, 4))
print("Context shape:", context.shape)
display(pd.DataFrame([
    ["Source of Q/K/V", "Same sequence projections", "Decoder state queries encoder states"],
    ["Attended items", "Every token can attend to every token", "One decoder state attends over encoder states"],
    ["Needs an RNN", "No", "Originally commonly paired with RNN encoder/decoder"],
    ["Parallelism", "All token pairs can be calculated together", "Often calculated per decoder step"],
    ["Where used", "Transformer encoder/decoder self-attention", "Encoder-decoder alignment/context"]
], columns=["Comparison", "Self-attention", "Luong dot attention"]))

Luong weights: [0.0476 0.1008 0.0008 0.6165 0.2343]
Context shape: (8,)
Comparison Self-attention Luong dot attention
0 Source of Q/K/V Same sequence projections Decoder state queries encoder states
1 Attended items Every token can attend to every token One decoder state attends over encoder states
2 Needs an RNN No Originally commonly paired with RNN encoder/de...
3 Parallelism All token pairs can be calculated together Often calculated per decoder step
4 Where used Transformer encoder/decoder self-attention Encoder-decoder alignment/context

Interpretation: Luong attention uses decoder information to focus on encoder states. Self-attention finds relationships between tokens in the same sequence.

Attention is order-blind¶

Without positional information, self-attention does not know the original order of tokens. Shuffling input rows should shuffle output rows in the same way.

In [14]:
perm = np.array([2, 0, 3, 1])
X_shuf = X[perm]
Q2, K2, V2 = X_shuf @ Wq, X_shuf @ Wk, X_shuf @ Wv
out_shuf = softmax(Q2 @ K2.T / np.sqrt(8)) @ V2
print("Outputs follow shuffled row order:", np.allclose(out_shuf, out[perm]))

Outputs follow shuffled row order: True

Interpretation: The output changes in the same way when the input order changes. This shows that self-attention alone does not understand word order.

Verify attention against DistilBERT¶

This cell recomputes layer-0, head-0 attention using DistilBERT's query and key projections. Small differences can occur because of implementation details or library versions, so the maximum difference is printed for inspection.

In [15]:
base_name = "distilbert-base-uncased"
base_tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(base_name)
base_model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(base_name, attn_implementation="eager")
base_model.eval()
sample = "The animal did not cross the street because it was tired."
inp = base_tok(sample, return_tensors="pt")
with torch.no_grad():
    result = base_model(**inp, output_hidden_states=True, output_attentions=True)
att = result.attentions[0][0, 0].cpu().numpy()
hidden = result.hidden_states[0]
layer = base_model.transformer.layer[0]
with torch.no_grad():
    q = layer.attention.q_lin(hidden)
    k = layer.attention.k_lin(hidden)
b, n, dim = q.shape
head_dim = dim // 12
q = q.view(b, n, 12, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
k = k.view(b, n, 12, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
manual_scores = q @ k.transpose(-1, -2) / math.sqrt(head_dim)
mask = (1.0 - inp["attention_mask"][:, None, None, :].float()) * -10000.0
manual_att = torch.softmax(manual_scores + mask, dim=-1)[0, 0].cpu().numpy()
diff = np.max(np.abs(manual_att - att))
print("Model attention shape:", att.shape)
print("Maximum absolute difference:", diff)
print("Close within 1e-4:", np.allclose(manual_att, att, atol=1e-4))

Task 3 — Multi-Head Attention, Positional Encoding and Layer Normalization¶

Multi-head attention¶

Each head has its own Query, Key and Value projections and can learn a different attention pattern. The head outputs are concatenated and mixed by an output projection; DistilBERT uses 12 heads of size 64, giving a hidden size of 768.

Interpretation: Multi-head attention uses several attention heads at the same time. Different heads can learn different word relationships.

Extract and plot real attention heads¶

In [16]:
head_text = "The animal did not cross the street because it was too tired."

Head diversity measurement¶

Low entropy means a head concentrates its attention on fewer tokens; high entropy means it spreads attention across more tokens. We compare the first and last encoder layers.

In [17]:

    ent = -(a * np.log(a + 1e-12)).sum(axis=-1).mean(axis=-1)
    for hi, val in enumerate(ent):

Sinusoidal positional encoding from scratch¶

Sinusoidal encoding gives each position a different pattern of sine and cosine values at multiple frequencies. These values are added to token embeddings to give attention information about order.

In [18]:
def positional_encoding(n_pos=50, d_model=128):
    pos = np.arange(n_pos)[:, None]
    dim = np.arange(d_model)[None, :]
    rates = 1 / np.power(10000, (2 * (dim // 2)) / d_model)
    angles = pos * rates
    pe = np.zeros((n_pos, d_model))
    pe[:, 0::2] = np.sin(angles[:, 0::2])
    pe[:, 1::2] = np.cos(angles[:, 1::2])
    return pe

pe = positional_encoding()
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 5))
sns.heatmap(pe, cmap="coolwarm", center=0)
plt.title("Task 3.4 — Sinusoidal Positional Encoding")
plt.xlabel("Dimension"); plt.ylabel("Position"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print("Encoding shape:", pe.shape)

Encoding shape: (50, 128)

Interpretation: Each row represents a word position and each column represents a feature. Sine and cosine values help represent word positions.

Position makes identical words different¶

Adding different positional vectors changes the representation of an otherwise identical word embedding. Cosine similarity compares the direction of the resulting vectors.

In [20]:
np.random.seed(42)
word = np.random.randn(128)
v3 = word + pe[3]
v20 = word + pe[20]
cos = lambda a, b: float(np.dot(a, b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b)))
print("Similarity without positional encoding:", cos(word, word))
print("Similarity at positions 3 and 20:", cos(v3, v20))

Similarity without positional encoding: 1.0000000000000002
Similarity at positions 3 and 20: 0.859478276443046

Interpretation: The same word has identical vectors before positional encoding. Adding different position vectors helps the model tell word positions apart.

Learned positional embeddings¶

DistilBERT learns position vectors instead of using the sinusoidal formula. This model has 512 learned position vectors; T5 uses relative position biases instead.

In [21]:
pos_weights = base_model.embeddings.position_embeddings.weight.detach().cpu().numpy()
print("Learned position embedding shape:", pos_weights.shape)
first64 = pos_weights[:64]
norms = np.linalg.norm(first64, axis=1, keepdims=True)
first64_norm = first64 / np.maximum(norms, 1e-12)
sim64 = first64_norm @ first64_norm.T
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 6))
sns.heatmap(sim64, cmap="coolwarm", center=0)
plt.title("Task 3.6 — Similarity of First 64 Learned Positions")
plt.xlabel("Position"); plt.ylabel("Position"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Learned position embedding shape: (512, 768)

Interpretation: The heatmap compares the model's learned position vectors. This DistilBERT model has position embeddings for up to 512 tokens.

LayerNorm from scratch¶

In [22]:
np.random.seed(42)
a = np.random.randn(4, 8)
eps = 1e-5
mean = a.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
var = a.var(axis=1, keepdims=True)
ln_np = (a - mean) / np.sqrt(var + eps)
ln_torch = torch.nn.LayerNorm(8, elementwise_affine=False)(torch.tensor(a, dtype=torch.float32)).numpy()
print("Per-token means:", ln_np.mean(axis=1))
print("Per-token standard deviations:", ln_np.std(axis=1))
print("Matches torch LayerNorm:", np.allclose(ln_np, ln_torch, atol=1e-5))

Per-token means: [-8.32667268e-17  2.77555756e-17 -5.55111512e-17  2.77555756e-17]
Per-token standard deviations: [0.99998939 0.99999209 0.99999424 0.99999325]
Matches torch LayerNorm: True

Interpretation: Layer normalization scales the features of each token. The NumPy result should be close to PyTorch's result.

LayerNorm vs BatchNorm¶

DistilBERT learns position vectors instead of using the sinusoidal formula. This model has 512 learned position vectors; T5 uses relative position biases instead.

In [23]:

print("BatchNorm per-token means:", np.round(bn.mean(axis=1), 4))

    ["Depends on batch size", "No", "Yes, in training"],

    ["Transformer usage", "Common", "Not the standard Transformer choice"]
], columns=["Point", "LayerNorm", "BatchNorm"]))

print("DistilBERT embedding LayerNorm gamma shape:", tuple(emb_ln.weight.shape))
print("DistilBERT embedding LayerNorm beta shape:", tuple(emb_ln.bias.shape))

BatchNorm per-token means: [ 0.6523 -0.3536 -0.1908 -0.1078]
Point LayerNorm BatchNorm
0 Normalized over Features within one token Batch/tokens for each feature
1 Depends on batch size No Yes, in training
2 Variable-length/padding Convenient per token Batch composition can affect statistics
3 Transformer usage Common Not the standard Transformer choice 
DistilBERT embedding LayerNorm gamma shape: (768,)
DistilBERT embedding LayerNorm beta shape: (768,)

Interpretation: LayerNorm normalizes features within each token. BatchNorm uses statistics across a batch, so the two methods behave differently.

Task 4 — Transformer Encoder Architecture and Masked Self-Attention¶

Encoder architecture¶

An encoder starts with token embeddings plus positional information. Each block applies multi-head self-attention, a residual connection and normalization, then a feed-forward network with another residual connection and normalization. In a bidirectional encoder, each token can attend to tokens on either side.

Interpretation: DistilBERT is an encoder model that reads context from both sides. GPT-style generation needs a mask so the model cannot see future tokens.

Print and read the real encoder¶

In [24]:
print(base_model)

    ["Token embedding", "embeddings.word_embeddings"],

    ["Feed-forward layers", "transformer.layer[i].ffn.lin1 / lin2"],

    ["Two block normalizations", "transformer.layer[i].sa_layer_norm / output_layer_norm"],

Where do the parameters live?¶

In [29]:
groups = {"Embeddings": 0, "Attention": 0, "Feed-forward": 0, "Layer norms": 0, "Classification head": 0, "Other": 0}
for name, p in clf_model.named_parameters():
    n = p.numel()
    if "embeddings" in name:
        groups["Embeddings"] += n
    elif any(x in name for x in ["q_lin", "k_lin", "v_lin", "out_lin"]):
        groups["Attention"] += n
    elif ".ffn." in name or "lin1" in name or "lin2" in name:
        groups["Feed-forward"] += n
    elif "LayerNorm" in name or "layer_norm" in name or "layernorm" in name:
        groups["Layer norms"] += n
    elif "classifier" in name or "pre_classifier" in name:
        groups["Classification head"] += n
    else:
        groups["Other"] += n
total = sum(groups.values())
group_df = pd.DataFrame([[k, v, 100*v/total] for k,v in groups.items()],

Masked (causal) self-attention from scratch¶

In [32]:
n = 6
causal_mask = np.triu(np.full((n, n), -np.inf), k=1)
np.random.seed(42)
raw_scores = np.random.randn(n, n)
causal_weights = softmax(raw_scores + causal_mask)
print("Causal mask:\n", causal_mask)
print("Row sums:", causal_weights.sum(axis=1))
plt.figure(figsize=(5, 4))
sns.heatmap(causal_weights, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="Blues")
plt.title("Task 4.6 — Causal Attention Mask")
plt.xlabel("Key position"); plt.ylabel("Query position"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Padding mask vS causal mask¶

The padding mask prevents attention to padding tokens. The causal mask prevents a token from looking ahead to future positions; they serve different purposes.

In [34]:

    ["Short sentence.", "This is a longer sentence with extra words for padding."],
    padding=True, return_tensors="pt"
)
with torch.no_grad():
    pad_out = base_model(**pad_batch, output_attentions=True)
pad_att = pad_out.attentions[-1].mean(dim=1).cpu().numpy()
print("Attention mask:\n", pad_batch["attention_mask"])
for i in range(2):
    pad_positions = (pad_batch["attention_mask"][i] == 0).nonzero(as_tuple=True)[0].tolist()
    if pad_positions:
        print("Example", i, "padding key positions:", pad_positions,
              "max received attention:", float(pad_att[i, :, pad_positions].max()))
display(pd.DataFrame([
    ["Purpose", "Ignore padding tokens", "Prevent looking at future tokens"],
    ["Pattern", "Mask key positions where attention_mask = 0", "Mask positions above diagonal"],
    ["Used by", "Encoder, decoder and encoder-decoder models as needed", "Autoregressive decoder self-attention"]
], columns=["Point", "Padding mask", "Causal mask"]))

Task 5 — Cross-Attention, Decoder Architecture and Inference¶

Decoder architecture¶

A classic Transformer decoder block uses masked self-attention, cross-attention to encoder outputs, and a feed-forward network, with residual connections and normalization. Encoder-only models focus on understanding, decoder-only models generate autoregressively, and encoder-decoder models can transform one sequence into another.

Interpretation: DistilBERT is an encoder, GPT-2 is a decoder, and T5 uses both. Each model type is designed for different text tasks.

Cross-attention¶

In cross-attention, Queries come from the decoder while Keys and Values come from the encoder output. This lets the decoder consult the source sentence while producing each target token, much like a decoder state attending over encoder states in Luong attention.

Interpretation: Cross-attention connects the input text with the output text. It helps the decoder focus on relevant input words.

Run an encoder-decoder model¶

In [43]:
from transformers import T5Tokenizer, T5ForConditionalGeneration

name = "t5-small"

tok = T5Tokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
model = T5ForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(name)

Extract and plot cross-attention¶

The expected French sentence is used as labels so the model can calculate cross-attention while the target labels are supplied. The heatmap averages the heads in the last decoder layer.

In [54]:
src_text = "translate English to French: The house is small."
target_text = "La maison est petite."
src_enc = t5_tok(src_text, return_tensors="pt")
target_enc = t5_tok(text_target=target_text, return_tensors="pt")
with torch.no_grad():
    t5_out = t5_model(
        input_ids=src_enc["input_ids"],
        attention_mask=src_enc["attention_mask"],
        labels=target_enc["input_ids"],
        output_attentions=True,
        return_dict=True
    )
cross = t5_out.cross_attentions[-1][0].mean(dim=0).cpu().numpy()
src_tokens = t5_tok.convert_ids_to_tokens(src_enc["input_ids"][0])
tgt_tokens = t5_tok.convert_ids_to_tokens(target_enc["input_ids"][0])
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
sns.heatmap(cross, xticklabels=src_tokens, yticklabels=tgt_tokens, cmap="viridis")
plt.title(" T5 Cross-Attention")
plt.xlabel("Input tokens"); plt.ylabel("Output tokens"); plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha="right"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print("Cross-attention shape:", cross.shape)

Cross-attention shape: (6, 11)

Interpretation: The heatmap shows how output tokens attend to input tokens. Word alignment may be useful, but it is not always one-to-one.

Inference is autoregressive — manual loop¶

In [49]:
prompt = "Artificial intelligence will"
ids = gpt_tok(prompt, return_tensors="pt")["input_ids"]
manual = ids.clone()
with torch.no_grad():
    for _ in range(20):
        logits = gpt_model(input_ids=manual).logits[:, -1, :]
        next_id = torch.argmax(logits, dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        manual = torch.cat([manual, next_id], dim=1)
manual_text = gpt_tok.decode(manual[0], skip_special_tokens=True)
with torch.no_grad():
    generated = gpt_model.generate(ids, max_new_tokens=20, do_sample=False)
generated_text = gpt_tok.decode(generated[0], skip_special_tokens=True)
print("Manual:", manual_text)
print("generate():", generated_text)
print("Identical:", torch.equal(manual, generated))

Manual: Artificial intelligence will be able to do things like search for and find people, and to do things like find out who
generate(): Artificial intelligence will be able to do things like search for and find people, and to do things like find out who
Identical: True

Interpretation: The manual loop generates one token at a time. With the same settings, it should match the model's greedy generation.

Decoding strategies¶

In [50]:
def generate_text(prompt, **kwargs):
    ids = gpt_tok(prompt, return_tensors="pt")["input_ids"]
    with torch.no_grad():
        out = gpt_model.generate(ids, max_new_tokens=40, **kwargs)
    return gpt_tok.decode(out[0], skip_special_tokens=True)

prompt = "Artificial intelligence will"
strategies = []
strategies.append(["Greedy", generate_text(prompt, do_sample=False)])
strategies.append(["Beam search", generate_text(prompt, do_sample=False, num_beams=5, early_stopping=True)])
for seed in [42, 43]:
    set_seed = torch.manual_seed(seed)
    strategies.append([f"Temperature 0.7 seed {seed}", generate_text(prompt, do_sample=True, temperature=0.7)])
for seed in [42, 43]:
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    strategies.append([f"Temperature 1.5 seed {seed}", generate_text(prompt, do_sample=True, temperature=1.5)])
torch.manual_seed(42)
strategies.append(["Top-k 50 + top-p 0.9", generate_text(prompt, do_sample=True, top_k=50, top_p=0.9, temperature=1.0)])
display(pd.DataFrame(strategies, columns=["Strategy", "Generated text"]))
Strategy Generated text
0 Greedy Artificial intelligence will be able to do thi...
1 Beam search Artificial intelligence will be the next big t...
2 Temperature 0.7 seed 42 Artificial intelligence will be used to create...
3 Temperature 0.7 seed 43 Artificial intelligence will help us learn how...
4 Temperature 1.5 seed 42 Artificial intelligence will continue to expan...
5 Temperature 1.5 seed 43 Artificial intelligence will help ensure that ...
6 Top-k 50 + top-p 0.9 Artificial intelligence will continue to expan...

Interpretation: Temperature controls how random the generated text can be. Top-k and top-p limit the possible next tokens.

KV-cache speed-up¶

The key and value vectors of earlier tokens do not change when generating later tokens. Caching them can avoid recomputing earlier states at every generation step.

In [51]:
def time_generation(use_cache, repeats=3):
    times = []
    ids = gpt_tok("Artificial intelligence will", return_tensors="pt")["input_ids"]
    for _ in range(repeats):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        with torch.no_grad():
            gpt_model.generate(ids, max_new_tokens=100, do_sample=False, use_cache=use_cache)
        times.append(time.perf_counter() - start)
    return float(np.mean(times)), times

cache_on, times_on = time_generation(True)
cache_off, times_off = time_generation(False)
print("use_cache=True average seconds:", round(cache_on, 3), "runs:", np.round(times_on, 3))
print("use_cache=False average seconds:", round(cache_off, 3), "runs:", np.round(times_off, 3))
print("Speed-up (no-cache time / cache time):", round(cache_off / max(cache_on, 1e-9), 2), "x")

use_cache=True average seconds: 3.315 runs: [3.522 3.168 3.255]
use_cache=False average seconds: 8.578 runs: [8.52  8.405 8.809]
Speed-up (no-cache time / cache time): 2.59 x

Interpretation: The timing depends on your computer. KV-cache can save time by reusing information from earlier tokens.

Cost grows with sequence length¶

We time a single DistilBERT forward pass for different input lengths, using one warm-up and ten timed runs per length. Small CPU measurements may look close to linear because other operations and overhead also contribute.

In [93]:
timing_rows = []
repeat_text = ("Transformers use attention to compare tokens in a sequence. " * 100)
for length in [32, 64, 128, 256, 512]:
    ids = base_tok(repeat_text, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, max_length=length)
    with torch.no_grad():
        base_model(**ids)
    run_times = []
    for _ in range(10):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        with torch.no_grad():
            base_model(**ids)
        run_times.append(time.perf_counter() - start)
    timing_rows.append([length, float(np.mean(run_times)), float(np.std(run_times))])
time_df = pd.DataFrame(timing_rows, columns=["Input length", "Mean seconds", "Std seconds"])
display(time_df)
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))
sns.lineplot(data=time_df, x="Input length", y="Mean seconds", marker="o")
plt.title("Forward-Pass Time vs Sequence Length")
plt.xlabel("Input tokens"); plt.ylabel("Mean seconds"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
Input length Mean seconds Std seconds
0 32 0.034143 0.002903
1 64 0.052876 0.002780
2 128 0.085255 0.002791
3 256 0.142751 0.017840

Interpretation: Attention compares tokens with one another, so longer text usually needs more computation. Small CPU tests may not show this clearly.

Hallucination check¶

GPT-2 is prompted for three factual continuations. Mark the output based on the generated answer; language models can produce fluent text without reliably verifying facts.

]

for p in fact_prompts:

    with torch.no_grad():
        out = gpt_model.generate(ids, max_new_tokens=30, do_sample=False)
    txt = gpt_tok.decode(out[0], skip_special_tokens=True)
    fact_outputs.append([p, txt, "Review manually: correct / partly correct / wrong"])

Build the mini application¶

In [101]:
def text_toolkit(text):
    if not isinstance(text, str) or not text.strip():
        return {
            "Sentiment": "N/A",
            "Score": 0.0,
            "Summary": "No text provided.",
            "French Translation": "No text to translate.",
            "Message": "Input is empty."
        }

    # Check input length
    full_ids = tok(
        text,
        add_special_tokens=True,
        truncation=False
    )["input_ids"]

    msg = "Processed successfully."

    if len(full_ids) > 512:
        msg = "Long input: truncated to 512 tokens."

    # Sentiment analysis
    sent = sentiment(
        text,
        truncation=True,
        max_length=512
    )[0]

    # Generate summary
    inp = tok(
        "summarize: " + text,
        return_tensors="pt",
        truncation=True,
        max_length=512
    )

    out = model.generate(
        **inp,
        max_length=60,
        min_length=10,
        do_sample=False
    )

    summary = tok.decode(
        out[0],
        skip_special_tokens=True
    )

    # Translate summary into French
    trans_inp = tok(
        "translate English to French: " + summary,
        return_tensors="pt",
        truncation=True,
        max_length=512
    )

    trans_out = model.generate(
        **trans_inp,
        max_length=60,
        do_sample=False
    )

    french = tok.decode(
        trans_out[0],
        skip_special_tokens=True
    )

    return {
        "Sentiment": sent["label"],
        "Score": round(sent["score"], 4),
        "Summary": summary,
        "French Translation": french,
        "Message": msg
    }

What I learned about Transformers¶

What I learned about Transformers :

(a) What I understand best

I understand how Transformers use tokenization, attention, and pretrained models to process text. I still need more practice understanding the attention mechanism and how each token attends to other tokens.

(b) Theory and practical observations

The model's sentiment predictions matched the theory that pretrained Transformers can classify text into positive and negative sentiment. One surprising thing was that changing the input length could change the prediction and the processing time.

(c) Two disadvantages observed

  1. Truncation: Short input limits can remove important information. At max_length 64, accuracy was ___, while at max_length 512, accuracy was ___. The accuracy difference was ___ percentage points.

  2. Processing time: Longer input sequences can take more time. The evaluation took ___ seconds at max_length 64 and ___ seconds at max_length 512. Also, ___ out of 200 reviews exceeded 512 tokens and lost some text due to truncation.

(d) Real-world application

I would build a movie review analysis application that predicts sentiment, summarizes reviews, and translates summaries into French. It would use an encoder-based model such as DistilBERT for sentiment classification and an encoder-decoder model such as T5 for summarization and translation.
